This group was re-sourced to the resort's own mountain statistics page once Vail's web estate came back up; the 29/47/24 split is identical to OnTheSnow's, which is mildly reassuring about both. The resort's own figures also corrected the acreage from 232 to 233 and, more usefully, supplied a snowmaking coverage of 97% where OnTheSnow had only an acreage. Note the longest run - 0.8 miles is the shortest on this roster, and on 1,510 feet of vertical that tells you the trails here fall steeply and end quickly rather than winding. Mount Sunapee sits inside Mount Sunapee State Park and is operated under a lease, which is why there is no slopeside development.

pricing.notes: 2026-27 season. Vail prices day tickets dynamically by date and publishes no fixed window rate, so the ticket fields are null rather than estimated. The season pass figure is the full adult (31+) Epic Pass; Vail does not sell an unrestricted Sunapee-only pass. Mount Sunapee carries unlimited access on the cheaper Epic Local Pass too, at $829 for 31+, which is the tier most New England Epic buyers actually want. mountsunapee.com's content pages became readable again on 2026-08-25 and this file was rebuilt from them, but its ticket and pass pages are a separate matter: every one of them redirects to Vail's ecommerce waiting room, which requires JavaScript. So the $1,119 still comes from OnTheSnow's Epic buyer's guide - its current-cost line, not its prose, which quotes the March 2026 on-sale price of $1,089.

editorial.overview: Mount Sunapee is the mountain that serves everything south and west of the White Mountains, and its virtue is that it is closer than the alternatives rather than better than them. Fifteen hundred and ten feet of vertical on 233 acres above Lake Sunapee, an hour and a half from Boston and well under that from Concord and the Upper Valley, on the Epic Pass at the unlimited tier on both the full pass and the Local. It sits inside Mount Sunapee State Park under a lease, which is why there is no village and no condominium sprawl - a genuinely pleasant thing, and the reason the base area still feels like a state park rather than a resort. The skiing is competent intermediate terrain, 47% of it blue, with a couple of real blacks off the summit and glades that mostly stay roped, and the South Peak learning area is one of the better dedicated beginner zones in the state. Snowmaking covers 97% of it, which it needs to. What holds Sunapee back is a combination of short runs - 0.8 miles is the shortest longest-run on this roster - modest snowfall, and weekend crowds that its two high-speed quads cannot absorb, with half-hour waits not unusual in the late morning. Midweek it is a good, quick, unfussy mountain. On a Saturday in February it is a queue with a view of the lake.
editorial.snowQuality: Ninety-three inches a year puts Mount Sunapee at about two-thirds of what the mountains in north-central New Hampshire get, though comfortably ahead of anything in Massachusetts, and the practical consequence is that this is a snowmaking mountain that occasionally gets a powder day rather than the other way round. The resort publishes 97% snowmaking coverage - among the highest on this roster - and that machine snow does the work all season, not just at the margins. The glades are the casualty: they rarely open, with ropes coming down only on powder days or in the few days after a real storm, so the tree skiing here should be treated as an occasional bonus rather than a reason to come.
editorial.crowds: The clearest weakness, and it is a capacity problem rather than a popularity one. Mount Sunapee draws a large weekend crowd from Boston, Concord and the Upper Valley, and its two high-speed quads become the bottleneck everything funnels through - waits of over half an hour are not out of the ordinary through the late morning and early afternoon on a Saturday. Unlimited access on the Epic Local Pass, which most New England Epic buyers hold, adds a passholder crowd on top of the day-ticket one. Midweek the mountain is a completely different and much better proposition. If your only option is a weekend, arrive at opening and take an early lunch.
editorial.difficulty: Comfortably intermediate with a thin top end. Forty-seven percent of the trails are blue and that is where the mountain lives; Upper Blast Off is the only black diamond directly off the summit, and Goosebumps - steep and ungroomed - is effectively the sole expert option. The advanced trails vary a lot in what they actually demand, with Upper Flying Goose and Lynx holding sustained pitch and seldom being groomed, which makes them the two worth seeking out. The glade terrain would add real difficulty if it were reliably open, and it is not. A strong skier will have seen everything Sunapee has by lunchtime; an improving intermediate will have a very good day.

keyTrails.name: Goosebumps
keyTrails.note: Steep and ungroomed, and effectively the only genuinely expert run on the mountain. Where Sunapee's small hard core spends its time.

keyTrails.name: Upper Flying Goose
keyTrails.note: Sustained pitch and seldom groomed, which makes it one of the two reliable places to find bumps here.

keyTrails.name: Lynx
keyTrails.note: The other seldom-groomed advanced trail, and the one that holds its pitch longest. Not to be confused with Wildcat's trail of the same name.

keyTrails.name: Upper Blast Off
keyTrails.note: The only black diamond dropping directly off the summit, which makes it the default first run of the day for anyone competent.

tidbits: Mount Sunapee sits inside Mount Sunapee State Park and is run under a lease, so there is no slopeside development.
The resort claims the world’s first ski-through lighthouse.
Thirteen other ski resort peaks are visible from the summit, by the resort’s own count.
At 0.8 miles, Sunapee’s longest run is the shortest on this roster.
It is unlimited on the Epic Local Pass as well as the full Epic Pass.
The glades open only on powder days or shortly after a real storm.
The resort’s own statistics page says 4 terrain parks; a tile on the same page says 2.
bestFor: A short drive from Concord or Boston

moguls.policy: Sunapee grooms most of what it can - a mountain covering 215 of 232 acres with snowmaking is protecting that surface - but leaves a small number of advanced trails alone. Upper Flying Goose and Lynx are seldom groomed and hold sustained pitch, and Goosebumps is ungroomed by default. That is three trails out of 67, which is the honest scale of it.

namedRuns.name: Goosebumps
namedRuns.note: Steep and ungroomed, and effectively Sunapee's only expert run. Reliably bumped because it is never groomed rather than because anyone maintains it as a bump line.

namedRuns.name: Upper Flying Goose
namedRuns.note: Seldom groomed and holding sustained pitch. Bumps up between passes and is one of the two places on the mountain where a strong skier finds something to do.

namedRuns.name: Lynx
namedRuns.note: The other seldom-groomed advanced trail. Not to be confused with Wildcat's Lynx, which is a considerably more serious proposition.

moguls.quality: Fine on its own terms and small in scope. Three trails is not a bump network, and none of them is long enough to be a real endurance test on 1,510 feet of vertical with a 0.8-mile longest run. What they have going for them is that they are ungroomed by default rather than by accident, so the moguls are actually there when you arrive - which is more than can be said for Gunstock, where the bumps depend on a nightly decision. The weekend crowding works against them too: heavy traffic on a short trail scrapes the troughs faster than the snow can rebuild.
moguls.bestTiming: Midweek, and late enough in the week for the weekend traffic to have been resurfaced by a storm or softened by sun. Spring is better than midwinter here, as at most low-snowfall mountains.
moguls.bumpCulture: None. Sunapee has no bump scene, no competitions, and a rider or skier looking for that culture in New Hampshire is at Waterville Valley instead.

parks.progression: Not documented as a ladder. What is known is that the beginner end sits on South Peak, separate from the main park off the Spruce Triple, which is a sensible split for a mountain whose learning area is its strongest feature - but the resort publishes nothing about how the steps between features work.
parks.overview: Sunapee publishes a park count and nothing else - no park page exists anywhere on mountsunapee.com, and a direct request for the terrain-parks URL its sister mountains use returns a 404. Worse, the resort contradicts itself on the same page: the mountain statistics block reads "Terrain Parks 4" while a Freestyle Fun tile a few hundred pixels below it says Sunapee "boasts 2 terrain parks each with a unique design and focus, from small progression features to large, expert level hits". The 4 is stored because the statistics block has been the reliable half of exactly this kind of self-contradiction elsewhere on this roster - it was right at Burke, where the prose was wrong - but the discrepancy is real and unresolved, and a reader should treat the count as approximate. Beyond the number, the only description available is third-party: PeakRankings describes one main park served by the Spruce Triple carrying boxes, rails and jumps, plus beginner features over on South Peak. No park names, no feature counts, no lighting and no rebuild schedule are published by anyone.
parks.reputation: Weak, and unusually bluntly so - the review consulted says outright that park rats should look elsewhere. That is a fair summary of a mountain that cannot say for certain how many parks it has and names none of them, on a site where its sibling Crotched gives both of its parks a page and a description. Anyone in this part of New Hampshire riding park seriously is at Waterville Valley or Loon, both within an hour and a half.
